title: Philosophy Through Arguments
description: A compact architecture fixture for a domain with alternative routes, primary texts, contrasts, and legitimate disagreement.

nodes.title: Reconstruct an argument charitably
nodes.summary: Identify premises, conclusion, implicit assumptions, and the strongest plausible form of an argument.

nodes.title: Compare competing philosophical positions
nodes.summary: Compare positions by their claims, reasons, objections, assumptions, and consequences without collapsing disagreement into preference.

nodes.title: Defend and revise a philosophical position
nodes.summary: Offer a reasoned position, answer a strong objection, and revise the claim when the objection exposes a real limitation.

nodes.title: Argument reconstruction diagnostic
nodes.summary: A short offline diagnostic for premise, conclusion, and charitable reconstruction.

mastery.instructions: Answer both argument-structure scenarios without hints.

questions.prompt: In ‘All policies that reduce avoidable harm deserve consideration; this policy reduces avoidable harm; therefore this policy deserves consideration,’ which clause is the conclusion?

options.label: All policies that reduce avoidable harm deserve consideration.

questions.prompt: A speaker argues: ‘The city should add protected bike lanes because safer routes bring more commuters to cycling, and fewer car trips reduce congestion.’ Which reconstruction is strongest and most charitable?

options.label: Cycling is good, so the city should eventually ban cars.

Protected lanes can make routes safer; safer routes can increase cycling; increased cycling can reduce car trips; fewer car trips can reduce congestion; therefore the city has a congestion-related reason to add protected lanes.
The city should add bike lanes because the speaker prefers bicycles.

nodes.title: Primary-text interpretation note
nodes.summary: A source-visible note separating text, context, interpretation, and evaluation.

mastery.instructions: Annotate a short primary passage with one quotation, its immediate context, a defensible interpretation, one alternative reading, and your separately labeled evaluation.

nodes.title: Comparative argument analysis
nodes.summary: A source-visible analysis of two competing positions and a defended revision.

mastery.instructions: Reconstruct two competing positions from primary or scholarly sources, state the strongest objection to each, and defend a revision while separating textual evidence from your evaluation.

edges.rationale: A comparison depends on representing each argument accurately before evaluating differences.
Primary-text interpretation strengthens comparison but some orientation routes can begin with reliable secondary sources.
Revision requires understanding live alternatives and objections rather than defending an isolated opinion.
A pathway may orient through a scholarly overview before or alongside direct primary-text study; neither substitutes universally for the other.
The free reference provides argument terminology and examples for reconstruction practice.
Scholarly entries provide historical context and bibliographies for primary-text interpretation.
Scholarly entries expose competing interpretations and bibliographies.
Scholarly surveys expose strong objections and live alternatives that inform defensible revision.
Repeated passage reconstruction practices premises, conclusions, assumptions, and charity.
Annotation makes the distinction between textual evidence, interpretation, and evaluation explicit.
Alternating positions and objections practices fair comparison before revision.
Alternating argument and objection makes revision visible as a capability.
Both offline scenarios must correctly identify structure and charitable reconstruction.
The annotated note demonstrates source-visible contextual interpretation.
The artifact requires accurate reconstruction and comparison.
The artifact includes a defended revision responsive to objections.
